1.
INTRODUCTION

[
1
]        The plaintiff seeks to set aside a release and claim damages
for injuries suffered in a motor vehicle accident.  Liability for the accident
is admitted.  The defendant opposes the application to set aside the release.
The issues are:

(1)  Was
the settlement and release signed by the plaintiff on June 3, 1991 fair, just
and reasonable?

(2)  If
not, and the release is set aside, has the plaintiff established on a balance
of probabilities that the negligence of the defendant caused the injuries he
says he has suffered?

(3)  If
he has, what monetary amount is appropriate to compensate the plaintiff for
those injuries?

2.
FACTS

(a)
THE ACCIDENT

[
2
]        The plaintiff, Vadim ("Jim") Gindis, a Russian
emigré, was injured in a motor vehicle accident on July 7, 1990 (the
"accident").  The defendant driver ran a red light at the
intersection of Georgia and Bute Streets in Vancouver, British Columbia.  Mr.
Gindis' vehicle was struck forcefully on the driver's side by the defendant's
vehicle in what is often described as a "T-bone" collision.  The
driver's door was caved in by the force of the impact.  Even though Mr. Gindis
was wearing a three point lap belt, his head struck the driver's side window
frame with such force that scratches remained on the moulding as did hair and
tissue from his scalp.

[
3
]        Liability for the accident is admitted.

[
4
]        At the scene of the accident, Mr. Gindis was dazed.  He does
not have a continuous memory of what occurred immediately after the collision.
He apparently drifted in and out of consciousness for approximately one hour.
He recalls trying to take a photograph.  He acted aggressively by pushing
people away.  He was bleeding profusely from his scalp.  He responded to
paramedics questions.  He describes the activity around him as "like a
dream"; his life history flashed by him "like a vision of a near
death experience."

[
5
]        He was transported by ambulance to St. Paul's Hospital.  His
Glasgow Coma Score of 15 was normal.  X-rays of his skull and neck were
negative.  The radiology notes indicated mild degenerative changes of the
L5-S1.  A 1.5 cm laceration on the left side of his scalp required five
stitches.  He initially did not recognize his wife, Florence George, when she
arrived at the hospital.  He spoke to her in Russian.  After five hours he was
sent home with head injury and wound care sheets.  Upon leaving the hospital,
over the objections of his wife, Mr. Gindis insisted on retrieving his car and
driving it home.

(b)
BACKGROUND

[
6
]        Mr. Gindis was born in Perm, Russia, on February 25, 1955.  His
parents, who were both physicians, separated when he was young.  His father was
of Jewish heritage and his mother was Russian.  His surname was uncommon in
Russia.  He was identified as Jewish because of his surname, although he was
not raised in the Jewish religion.  This perceived Jewish background caused him
some discrimination in Russia.

[
7
]        His natural father eventually immigrated to Israel.  His mother
remarried and he grew up in a home that included a stepfather and two older
stepbrothers.  He had a happy childhood and young adult life in Russia.

[
8
]        Mr. Gindis graduated from high school in 1974.  Perm is an
industrial city, and after graduation Mr. Gindis attended a polytechnical
institute.  In 1975 he obtained his qualifications as an electrical and gas
welder.  This occupation was in demand in Russia and attracted a good salary.

[
9
]        Mr. Gindis describes welding as physically demanding and
stressful.  His work involved heavy lifting and carrying equipment parts.  He
used his hands all the time.  As a fabricator, he had to read blueprints and
then assemble pieces of equipment in accordance with them.  For these reasons,
he kept himself physically fit by playing sports.  He abstained from alcohol
consumption and to this date does not drink.

[
10
]       After leaving the polytechnical institute, Mr. Gindis developed
a close friendship with Vladimir Ilinsky.  Mr. Ilinsky immigrated to Canada in
1987.  Upon his arrival in Canada he found steady continuous employment and now
owns and operates his own painting business.  He was a witness at this trial.

[
11
]       Between 1975 and 1979 Mr. Gindis was employed at a number of
jobs.  At his request, he was discharged from five of the twelve jobs he held
during that period.  The last discharge on February 19, 1979 occurred when he
accepted his natural father's invitation to be repatriated to Israel as a
Jewish person.

[
12
]       In April 1979 Mr. Gindis immigrated to Israel.  He obtained work
as a welder.  He states he again experienced discrimination this time because
he was a non-practising Jew.

[
13
]       Shortly after his arrival in Israel, Mr. Gindis travelled to
Greece, Rome, Austria and the Hague.  In each of these places he applied at the
Canadian Embassy for permission to enter Canada as a landed immigrant.  The
application he filed in Vienna, Austria, was rejected by Immigration Canada on
January 16, 1981.  Mr. Gindis did not receive notification of the rejection.
Mr. Gindis remained in Israel for two years and became an Israeli citizen with
an Israeli passport.  His passport was valid until 1985.

[
14
]       In the fall of 1982, Mr. Gindis arrived as a visitor in
Vancouver, British Columbia.  He says he came to Canada to follow up on his
immigration application.  He applied for refugee status, but was refused and
ordered deported by January 30, 1983.  Over the next two years he was
embroiled in a lengthy appeal process to the Immigration Appeal Board, the
Federal Court of Canada, the Federal Court of Appeal, and the Supreme Court of
Canada.

[
15
]       To assist his immigration application, on October 21, 1982, Mr.
Gindis obtained a letter of reference and offer of employment from a business,
Auto Rebuild.  This letter confirmed that he had valuable employment skills for
the business.  He worked a couple of months for Auto Rebuild repairing cars.
His pay was minimal.

[
16
]       From 1982 to 1983 Mr. Gindis took odd jobs obtained through the
Russian Community Centre.  His limited English language skills posed some
impediment to finding satisfactory work.  He painted, cleaned apartments,
landscaped, mowed lawns, and pruned trees.  At the end of 1983 he applied for
and received social assistance.  He completed a beginners English course and
typing course at King Edward Campus.  These courses were sponsored by social
assistance.  On March 8, 1984, he obtained his Registered "A" Welder
Certificate.

[
17
]       Mr. Gindis met his first wife, Florence George, at the Russian
Community Centre in 1983.  She was a social worker with the Ministry of Social
Services.  They dated for approximately two years and were married on December
23, 1985.  In 1984, Ms. George helped Mr. Gindis obtain a work permit from the
Department of Citizenship and Immigration ("Immigration").  She paid
$300.00 for him to join the welder's union after he obtained his Class
"A" Certificate.

[
18
]       On February 13, 1986 the Immigration Appeal Board made a final
ruling.  It rejected Mr. Gindis' application for convention refugee status.
His Israeli passport had expired by this date.

[
19
]       Mr. Gindis then applied for landed immigrant status based on his
marriage to Ms. George.  Immigration officials interviewed Mr. Gindis and Ms.
George, suspicious that theirs was a marriage of convenience.  It quickly
became apparent to them that the relationship was authentic.  Mr. Gindis was
granted landed immigrant status based on his marriage to Ms. George.  However,
Ms. George was required to financially sponsor Mr. Gindis for ten years.

[
20
]       Mr. Gindis' receipt of social assistance ended on his marriage
to Ms. George.  She became his source of support.  She paid all of the
household bills.  Mr. Gindis spent his limited income on his own personal
expenses including clothing and car payments.  He also paid a few utility
bills.  Within two years the couple purchased a condominium in Richmond.  The
home was registered in joint names; however, Ms. George made all of the
mortgage payments.

[
21
]       Mr. Gindis had very limited work from 1983, when he obtained his
work permit, to the date of the accident on July 7, 1990.  After 1984, he
worked on call for Geneva Language Institute Ltd. ("Geneva") as an
interpreter and translator of the Russian, Hebrew and English languages.  In
1985 he was certified as an Official Court Interpreter in the Russian
language.  Mr. Janulus, the owner of Geneva, described Mr. Gindis as an affable,
friendly, outgoing and conscientious worker up to 1990.

[
22
]       Mr. Gindis obtained his first welding job in Canada on October

Most of Mr. Gindis'
welding jobs ended due to work shortage.

[
23
]      Mr. Gindis suffered a workplace accident on June 5, 1989 (the
"WCB accident") at Progressive Marine Ltd.
("Progressive").  He had been employed as a welder fabricator in a
shipyard and had fallen from staging.  His head hit the floor, he lost
consciousness, bruised his ribs, injured his right shoulder, and experienced
low back pain which radiated down into his left leg.  After the WCB accident he
lost the Progressive and Aco jobs because of his slower work production.

[
24
]      His last job before the accident was with Sonic Barrier Sound
Products, of Delta, B.C. ("Sonic").  He had commenced employment with
Sonic three days before the accident.  He earned $17.20/hr as a metal
fabricator.  Sonic was a job shop and there was no guarantee of continued
availability of work.  While Mr. Doer, the owner of Sonic, did not specifically
recall Mr. Gindis, he did remember that on learning of his accident he felt
that he had lost a good employee.  Mr. Doer also confirmed that there was a
demand for welders with "A" certificates.  In order to qualify for
the job, Mr. Gindis was pre-screened and had to successfully complete a written
test.  The job required that he be able to read blueprints and follow
drawings.  There was a two week probationary period.  His work with Sonic ended
after three days because of the accident.

[
25
]      Mr. Gindis' income tax returns for 1987 and 1990 reflect the

[
27
]      During his marriage to Ms. George, Mr. Gindis expressed a
continued interest in doing something else.  He told Ms. George that he did not
like the working conditions for a welder.  He looked into forestry but the
entry list was too long and they could not afford the course.

[
28
]      Mr. Gindis' low back pain from the WCB accident continued to
affect his physical activities and ability to work as a welder.  He had decided
before the accident to change occupations due to this ongoing injury. Through
her contact with the Ministry of Social Services, Ms. George arranged for him
to take the business English course.  She also encouraged him to attend the
BCIT course.  She was involved in the planning and upgrading of his education
and training.

[
29
]      Ms. George supported Mr. Gindis until their marital separation in
December 1990.

(c)
THE CIRCUMSTANCES LEADING UP TO RELEASE

[
30
]      On July 10, 1990, three days after the accident, Mr. Gindis went
to I.C.B.C. to provide a written statement of the accident circumstances and
file a claim regarding his injuries.  He met with bodily injury adjuster Sherry
Levinson.  She was suspicious of his claim when he arrived wearing a large
white bandage around his head.  She did not think the size of the laceration
warranted such treatment.

[
31
]      Mr. Gindis complained of a sore back, neck, legs, chest and left
side of his body.  He said he felt restless, disoriented and could not
concentrate.  He asked Ms. Levinson for copies of all the documents he signed.
These included his statement to I.C.B.C. and medical and Unemployment Insurance
Commission ("UIC") authorizations for release of information.  He
told her he made that request because of the medication he was on, suggesting
he might not be responsible.  Ms. Levinson told him he could return another
day, but he replied that he felt fine.  Ms. Levinson, in her CL-80 notes,
recorded that Mr. Gindis was "very claims conscious and didn't appear to
comprehend a lot.  He doesn't really answer questions, but goes on and
on."  She further noted that Mr. Gindis ". . . may be priming us for
head injury claim . . ."

[
32
]      On July 13, 1990, Ms. Levinson spoke to Sonic.  She was advised
that due to Mr. Gindis' limited employment, he did not qualify for sick leave
or long term disability benefits.

[
33
]      Dr. Richards, Mr. Gindis' family doctor, first saw Mr. Gindis
following the accident on July 16, 1990.  Mr. Gindis complained of pain on the
top left side of his skull (he had stitches to the skull laceration on the
vault of his skull), sternomastoid pain going down to his ears, pain on the
right side at the vault of his skull, soreness in both shoulders, numbness over
the deltoid muscle, discomfort above the elbows, central chest pains, pains
from the suprapubic region up to the lower part of the chest cage, and pain in
the left buttock (which he had before the accident) that went further down the
left leg.  He had some right leg pain and bruising above the right knee as
well.  He had pain throughout his body from his head to his knees.

[
34
]      The WCB accident had caused him some degenerative disc disease
and ongoing low back pain.  Dr. Richards had given him an exercise therapy
program that he had completed and that had apparently improved his backache.
Before the accident, this backache occurred generally only in the morning.  His
low back pain was aggravated by the accident.

[
35
]      Dr. Richards advised Mr. Gindis to stop laying around the house.
He recommended Mr. Gindis attend a physiotherapy clinic, Hughes - Cross
Associates.  This clinic is located in Richmond, close to where Mr. Gindis
resided.  He warned him that lack of activity would result in deconditioning
and that he should walk every day on an increasing basis and ride his bicycle.
Mr. Gindis attempted this but continued to experience pain.  Dr. Richards
prescribed Doloboid for Mr. Gindis' pain.

[
36
]      On July 18, 1990, Mr. Gindis again met with Ms. Levinson.  He
complained of headaches, numbness from pelvis to legs, and a sore neck.  He
also stated that he could not concentrate or work.  She recorded: "still
seems confused and slow (in head)."  She cannot recall if Mr. Gindis told
her this or if this was her impression of him.  She also noted:  "He
looked fine, however."  On the same date she sent an internal message to
the defendant's adjuster requesting a copy of the defendant's statement and the
police report.  She volunteered that she had "an injury claim here and
probably a relatively large one."

[
37
]      On July 23, 1990, when Mr. Gindis was in to see her about repairs
to his vehicle, she noted:  "He doesn't understand me so told him to call
shop."

[
38
]      Dr. Richards completed the CL-19 report to I.C.B.C. on July 23, 1990.
He noted that Mr. Gindis was not working before the accident due to the WCB
accident.

[
39
]      Dr. Richards did not know Mr. Gindis had been employed before the
accident as a welder for Canadian Rubber and Steel Ltd. ("Canadian")
from April 2, 1990 to June 17, 1990 and as a metal fabricator for Sonic
from July 7 - 10, 1990.  He believed that after the WCB accident, when he first
saw Mr. Gindis as a patient in January 1990, Mr. Gindis had been let go from
two jobs.  He understood Mr. Gindis had been unemployed since January 1990 and
had refused to return to work after the WCB accident even though he had been
assessed fit enough to do so.  Dr. Richards' understanding of Mr. Gindis'
pre-accident employment was inaccurate.

[
40
]      Dr. Richards stated it was difficult to separate Mr. Gindis'
injuries between the two accidents.  He told Ms. Levinson that Mr. Gindis had
experienced similar physical problems from the WCB accident.  His prognosis
from the accident was "guarded" with instructions that Mr. Gindis
"have regular exercise program and inculcation of regular work
attendance."

[
41
]      Ms. Levinson wrote to Dr. Richards on August 3, 1990 to request a
detailed narrative medical report.

[
42
]      By August 1990 Mr. Gindis was still unable to work.  He continued
to experience headaches, neck and back pain.  He attended physiotherapy two
times per week.  He did not qualify for UIC.  On August 28, 1990, he told Ms.
Levinson that before the accident he had earned approximately $2,000.00 per
month.  He stated that his wife worked.  Her income, he said, went to pay
certain expenses, and he needed money to pay his mortgage and other expenses.

[
43
]      Ms. Levinson received written information from the Canada
Employment Centre that Mr. Gindis had collected Unemployment Insurance from
December 24, 1989 to April 7, 1990 and from June 10, 1990 to July 7, 1990.  He
did not qualify for sickness benefits.

[
44
]      Mr. Gindis continued to receive the weekly wage indemnity from
I.C.B.C. ("TTD"); however, Ms. Levinson told him that these benefits
would stop as soon as she received a report from his family doctor indicating
that he should be back to work.

[
45
]      In September 1990, Mr. Gindis told Ms. Levinson he was broke and
needed money.  His wife had told him that she intended to separate.  Ms.
Levinson received authorization to advance Mr. Gindis $2,000.00; however, she
recorded in her notes:  "obviously, he is ready to take advantage of the
system."  The claims review committee instructed Ms. Levinson to
investigate Mr. Gindis' personal and employment background and to do "some
surveillance".  The surveillance report received in November 1990 from a
private investigator and video crew provided no evidence to support Ms.
Levinson's suspicions.

[
46
]      On September 12, 1990, Ms. Levinson again spoke with Dr.
Richards.  She made the following notes of their telephone conversation:

1.   This guy will be a problem - chronic pain
person;

2.   He is still putting him through tests for head
injury;

3.   Jim is very passive-aggressive.  He has poor
motivation and is introspective;

4.   Jim could and should be doing housework and
exercise;

5.   Jim should try to go back to work but he
probably won't;

6.   Jim hates welding;

7.   It would be best to force Jim to go for
treatment with, for example, Worker's Compensation Board (WCB).

[
47
]      In cross-examination, Dr. Richards admitted that Mr. Gindis never
actually said that he hated welding or that he wanted to stop welding.

[
48
]      Ms. Levinson contacted the Workers' Compensation Board on
September 18, 1990 to ask about their work hardening program.  They advised her
they had no program to offer Mr. Gindis and, in any event, did not want to get
involved due to the possibility of a court action.  On October 18, 1990 she
noted that Dr. Richards was to give her information on a possible
rehabilitation program for Mr. Gindis.

[
49
]      In October of 1990 Ms. Levinson went on maternity leave.  Before
transferring the file, her final note of October 19, 1990 states:  "TTD
should be paid until confirm with doctor - by phone or report - that he should
be working . . . Rule out head injury problem".

[
50
]      It was under this cloud of suspicion recorded in Ms. Levinson's
CL-80 notes that, on October 25, 1990, Mr. Gindis' file was transferred to a
new adjuster, Mr. Larry Laws.  He had been employed by I.C.B.C. as a bodily
injury adjuster since March 1990.

[
51
]      Ms. Levinson could not specifically recall if she had met with
Mr. Laws to review the file, but she assumes she did.  She stated that during
the meeting she would have discussed her impression of Mr. Gindis, as Mr. Laws
would not have met him.  Mr. Laws' notes of October 25, 1990 were made when he
reviewed Ms. Levinson's file.  These notes indicate he intended to discuss the
CL-80 notes with Ms. Levinson.

[
52
]      After reviewing Ms. Levinson's file, Mr. Laws recorded:  "It
appears Dr. agrees the claimant is not motivated to return to work."

[
53
]      In fact, after the WCB accident, Mr. Gindis had voluntarily
returned to work with Progressive within a month.  He experienced difficulty
with the work because of his back injury, and his employment ended on August 4,
1989.

[
54
]      By September 1990 Mr. Gindis' continuing neck pain was resulting
in headaches severe enough to cause him to vomit.  Mr. Gindis stated that he
could not do physical work, such as painting and lifting around his home,
without assistance.  Dr. Richards made it clear to Mr. Gindis that in his
opinion he could do the necessary painting and housework.  He refused to
sanction Mr. Gindis' request for assistance with these tasks.

[
55
]      Mr. Gindis experienced depression and lost weight.  Prior to the
accident he had been depressed over financial and marital problems.  Dr.
Richards had referred him to Dr. Paragas in February of 1990.  Dr. Paragas had
concluded that Mr. Gindis was not clinically depressed, but might benefit from
marital counselling.  Dr. Richards had prescribed Prozac and continued to
prescribe this medication to Mr. Gindis after the accident until Mr. Gindis
told him he felt better.  Surprisingly, Mr. Gindis stated that after a week he
had stopped taking the Prozac Dr. Richards continued to prescribe for him.

[
56
]      Dr. Richards was of the opinion that at least six months before
the accident, Mr. Gindis' depression and low back pain had improved with
treatment.  Ms. George also confirmed that four weeks after the WCB accident
Mr. Gindis appeared sufficiently recovered to return to work.  On June 13 and
18, 1990, Mr. Gindis had two physiotherapy treatments for his low back pain.
He received these treatments after he had completed 11 weeks of medium to heavy
welding employment with Canadian.  He received no complaints on his work.  His
employment ended due to work shortage.  On cross-examination,  Dr. Richards
agreed there was no indication Mr. Gindis was trying to capitalize on his low
back pain to stay out of work in June 1990.

[
57
]      On September 26, 1990, Dr. Mark Lee, a radiologist at Lions Gate
Hospital, gave Mr. Gindis a CAT scan.  He reported the results as normal with no
evidence of subdural haematoma.

[
58
]      Mr. Gindis continued to complain of frequent  headaches on both
the front and top of his head going back to his neck.  He had nausea, vertigo,
and decreased reaction time.  He could not think quickly and complained of
decreased comprehension.  These symptoms frightened him.  He continued to have
low back pain on his left side radiating from his buttock to his knee.  He
complained of numbness and paraesthesia in his left hand.

[
59
]      By October 1990 Mr. Gindis' condition remained unchanged.  Dr.
Richards felt that Mr. Gindis' inactivity was compounding the problem.  He
communicated this to Ms. Levinson and recommended an immediate work assessment
and work hardening program.  Ms. Levinson told Dr. Richards that she could not
find a sponsor for such a program.  She understood the issue was left with Dr.
Richards to search out an appropriate program for Mr. Gindis.  Dr. Richards understood
I.C.B.C. was looking into this.

[
60
]      In his October 17, 1990 letter to I.C.B.C., Dr. Richards
summarized his opinion of Mr. Gindis' condition:

I
am uncertain as to the length of time of his total or partial disability.  In
view of his dislike of his job (indeed, Mr. Gindis certainly does not dress,
look, or talk like a welder and I think finds himself probably out of sympathy
with his workmates) I think this is the classical case of a worker who is
possibly seeking a way out from his current work.  Indeed, given the severity
of physical injuries and previous problems, a change in his occupation is in
his best interests.  In view of the history of marginal employment since his
Workers' Compensation injury, I would have to question return to his current
occupation.  The fact that neither employment duties nor leisure activities
have been affected differentially, it does indicate that this worker has sustained
a fair degree of physical insult.  Until we deal with the depression and his
problems with his motivation and adaptation to Western life, I don't think we
can see a way forward with this patient.  I have indicated to him that a return
to a regular work scenario is vital.

If
we do not get this patient into a work hardening program we will lose this
patient to frustration and long term unemployment.  I think he should be put
into the Workers' Compensation rehabilitation system if that is possible on
contract so that he undertake regular work; and assessment of his job and
alternative skills be made quickly and a vigorous rehabilitation programme
worked out for him with a muscle strengthening regime which he would be
required and paid to do.

In trying to apportion the
various physical injuries to his motor vehicle or his Workers'
Compensation-related injury, I would have to say that all upper back problems
are a result of this accident; whereas the low back discomfort is an aggravation
of pre-existing degenerative disc disease precipitated by the fall from the
staging.

Despite vigorous
rehabilitation attempts, I would remain pessimistic about the patient's

FINDINGS OF FACT

[
161

diagnoses and prognoses from a variety of specialists.  On a balance of
probabilities, I make the following findings:

1.   Mr. Gindis suffered a mild, traumatic head injury
(concussion) from the accident.  He has no apparent residual physical or
objective symptoms from the head injury.

2.   Since the accident Mr. Gindis has experienced chronic
pain, a condition most of the specialists have described as CPS.  His ongoing
pain has resulted in physical, emotional, and cognitive impairment, all of
which are psychologically and emotionally based.  He has no residual physical,
emotional or cognitive impairment from the head injury.

3.   Mr. Gindis presents no signs of exaggerated pain
behaviour, conscious secondary gain, or malingering.

4.   Mr. Gindis is not clinically depressed, but instead
suffers from a mood of depression and anxiety that arises from the chronic pain
and that he masks by a focus on his physical symptoms.  He was not clinically
depressed before the accident.

5.   Mr. Gindis had pre-existing paranoid and narcissistic
personality traits (not a psychiatric disorder as defined by the DSM-IV Manual)
which may have contributed to or exacerbated his present condition of CPS.
There is no evidence that Mr. Gindis was psychologically or socially
dysfunctional before the accident.

6.   Mr. Gindis had pre-existing low back pain radiating
down into his buttock and left leg.  This backache was aggravated by the
accident.  He continues to experience this same low back pain.

7.   Mr. Gindis' lack of exercise, due to his fear of
reinjury and his belief that he continues to suffer from an organic head
injury, has resulted in a deconditioning of his muscles and has contributed to
his present state of chronic pain.

8.   Mr. Gindis requires therapeutic, psychiatric or
psychological treatment, outside the scope of litigation, where a trust
relationship can develop between himself and his therapist.  He also requires
participation in a work-hardening and pain management program in order to learn
how to refocus away from his complaints of pain to the type of work he is able
to do.

9.   Mr. Gindis' prognosis for a return to employment
depends upon his motivation to do something about his present condition.  His
successful completion of the NOW program and Vancouver School Board computer
courses, as well as his commitment to raising his child, have improved the
original guarded prognosis.

10.  By January 1991 Mr. Gindis was able to return to light
employment provided it did not require substantial concentration.

ANALYSIS

(a)
ISSUE 1: IS THE RELEASE BINDING

[
162
] The authorities that establish the test to be applied in deciding
whether a bargain is unconscionable and warrants the equitable relief of being
set aside were thoroughly canvassed by Taylor J.A. in
Smyth
v. Szep
(1992), 63 B.C.L.R. (2d) S2 (C.A.).  More recently, they have
been reviewed by Oppal J. in
McCullough v. Hilton

(Q.L.
1997 B.C.J. No. 4657 (B.C.S.C.)
.  In both of these cases, the release was
the result of an unconscionable bargain and, therefore, found to be not binding
on the plaintiff.

[
163
] There will be a presumption that a bargain is unconscionable in the
following circumstances:

1.   Where there was inequality in the position of the
parties due to ignorance, need or distress of the weaker which would leave him
in the power of the stronger, and

2.   Proof of substantial unfairness in the bargain based
on the circumstances known or within the means of knowledge of the stronger at
the time.

On proof of these
circumstances the onus will shift to the stronger to show that the bargain was
fair, just and reasonable if the bargain is to be preserved:
Morrison v. Coast Finance Ltd.
(1965),
1965 CanLII 493 (BC CA)
, 54 W.W.R. 257
(B.C.C.A.);
Harry v. Kneutziger
(1978),
1978 CanLII 393 (BC CA)
, 9 B.C.L.R.
166 (C.A.).

[
164
] In
Cougle v. Maricevic

(1983), 64 B.C.L.R.
105 (C.A.)
, Lambert J.A. stated that where a bargain was not "fair"
on the basis of what was known to the adjuster or within his means of knowledge
at the time, in the absence of special circumstances, it will be found to
"diverge so greatly from community standards of commercial morality that
it should be rescinded."  Taylor J.A. further expanded on this theme in
Smyth v. Szep
,
supra
, at 63,
where he stated:

The
community should, in my view, be taken to expect adherence to a high standard
of commercial morality of a Crown corporation exercising a monopoly function of
this sort in settling claims with members of the public which it serves.  While
efficiency is, of course, properly expected of such a government enterprise, it
would in my view be wrong to assume that the insurance corporation is expected
to take unfair advantage of inexperienced and unadvised claimants.  They are,
after all, persons for whose benefit the scheme exists.

[
165
] Monopoly powers import enhanced responsibilities to treat fairly those
over whom the monopoly extends.  Our society has developed various regulatory
mechanisms to temper potentially unfair behaviour rooted in the power of
monopoly.  However, where regulation has not existed, the common law has
accommodated the need to access justice in an impartial forum.

1990, Dr. Richards' initial CL-19 report to I.C.B.C. of October 17, 1990 which
Mr. Wirth had obtained from Mr. Laws, Dr. Richards' medical-legal report of
March 27, 1991, and the St. Paul's Hospital records.

[
171
] In these circumstances, I conclude that Mr. Gindis was clearly the
weaker party.  There was an obvious disparity in the bargaining positions.
Even though an insurance adjuster is an employee of I.C.B.C., where a party is
unrepresented, there is at least a duty to disclose all available medical and
other information that forms the basis of the offer to settle.  Without such
disclosure, no party can make an informed decision on the fairness of the
offer.

[
172
] The court must next determine whether, despite the disparity in the
bargaining positions, the settlement was a fair one.  This depends upon what
information Mr. Laws actually knew regarding the medical condition of Mr.
Gindis as well as what information Mr. Laws would have discovered if he made
reasonable inquiries.

[
173
] Mr. Laws relied on selective subjective statements from Dr. Richards'
October 17, 1990 report and telephone conversations and took the position that
Mr. Gindis had only sustained a minor soft tissue injury from the accident and
was able to return to work as a welder by September 1990.  In so doing, he
ignored other statements in the report from which one could conclude that Mr.
Gindis' recovery from a severe physical trauma might not have been complete at
that time.  He also ignored Dr. Ciszak's notes of December 17, 1990 and April
18, 1991.

[
174
] In addition, Mr. Laws chose to ignore additional medical information
he could have obtained from Dr. Ciszak's file, including reports from Dr.
Paragas, Dr. Paton, Dr. Matkin, Dr. Coughlan, Dr. Wilkinson, and the
Hughes-Cross Physiotherapy Clinic.  All of this information indicated Mr.
Gindis had ongoing problems that required further investigation.  Whether or
not these ongoing problems would be permanent was unknown at that time.

[
175
] Mr. Laws chose not to extend his inquiry beyond Dr. Richards' letter
of October 17, 1990.  He did this in order to obtain a quick settlement for
less than estimated by the claims review committee in its suggested reserves.

[
176
] By the time the Release was signed, the claims review committee had
increased its reserve estimate from a low of $19,500.00 to a high of
$31,924.00.  Both reserve estimates apportioned a sum of money for past wage
loss.  Yet Mr. Laws made no inquiry into Mr. Gindis' employment background or
his future employment prospects with Sonic had the accident not occurred.  If
Mr. Gindis had continued in that employment to the date of the Release
(although such an assumption is highly speculative), his wage loss claim alone
would have been more than the settlement amount.  Dr. Richards' had recommended
that Mr. Gindis participate in a work hardening program as soon as possible.
This was never discussed with Mr. Gindis.

[
177
] Defendant's counsel has referred to a number of decisions of this
court in support of their position that at the time the Release was signed, a
soft tissue injury, with a pre-existing condition, was worth between $8,000.00
and $35,000.00, depending on the circumstances.  All of these cases were
decided from 1989 to 1991 and pre-date the Court of Appeal decisions of
Maslen v. Rubenstein
(1993),
1993 CanLII 2465 (BC CA)
, 83 B.C.L.R. (2d) 131 (C.A.),

Skelton v. Stewart
(1994),
1994 CanLII 3165 (BC CA)
, 93 B.C.L.R. (2d) 200
(C.A.), and
Yoshikawa v. Yu
(1996),
1996 CanLII 3104 (BC CA)
, 21 B.C.L.R.
(3d) 318 (C.A.).  These latter decisions address the issue of compensation for
cases of chronic pain.  Of course, in June of 1991, there was no suggestion
that Mr. Gindis permanently suffered from chronic pain, although Dr. Richards'
somewhat prophetic statement hinted that this was a possibility unless Mr.
Gindis immediately participated in a work hardening program.

[
178
] I do not find these earlier decisions helpful as the awards therein
were based on medical prognoses that did not suggest ongoing problems related
to the accident.  They involve plaintiffs who had returned or had the ability
to return to their pre-accident employment.  The medical opinions for Mr.
Gindis did not recommend a return to his employment as a welder fabricator.
Furthermore, many of the decisions awarded additional damages for past and
future income loss.  As Mr. Gindis' settlement was a global one, it is
difficult to compare the cases.

[
179
] Mr. Laws' notes reveal that his goal was as much to avoid or limit
coverage as to fairly determine the claim as between the insurer and the
insured.  On the whole of the evidence, I find the settlement in June of 1991
to have been premature and unfair to Mr. Gindis.

[
180
] The Release may still be enforceable, however, if on all of the
evidence available to the parties at this time, the defendant can show the
settlement was fair, just and reasonable.  Such a determination will
necessarily involve an analysis of Mr. Gindis' personal and employment
background, as well as events subsequent to the settlement.  In short, the
court must determine an appropriate level of compensation for injuries such as
those suffered by Mr. Gindis in order to decide if the settlement was fair in
all the circumstances.  For that reason, I shall delay my ultimate decision on
this issue until I determine the appropriate level of compensation on the facts
before me.

(b)
ISSUE 2: CAUSATION

[
181
] Causation is the primary issue in assessing whether the losses claimed
by Mr. Gindis are compensable.

[
182
] The plaintiff submits that his present condition of CPS and inability
to work is a direct result of the accident.  The defendant argues the
following.  Mr. Gindis suffered a soft tissue injury from the accident from
which he was recovered by October 1990.  He has no objective physical,
emotional, or cognitive problems from his head injury.  His present
dysfunctional state pre-existed the accident and is due to paranoid and
narcissistic personality traits of a dependent personality.  His ongoing low
back pain and any depression he presently suffers also pre-existed the
accident.  In sum, if Mr. Gindis does suffer from CPS, it is not causally
connected to the accident.

[
183
] I have reviewed the medical evidence and the evidence from the lay
witnesses who knew Mr. Gindis both before and after the accident.  My findings
do not support the defendant's position.

[
184
] This Court has approached with caution, the making of awards for pain
and suffering in the absence of objective evidence of continuing injury and
where complaints of pain have persisted beyond the normal period of recovery.
There must be evidence of a "convincing" nature to overcome the
improbability that pain will continue in the absence of objective evidence of
continuing injury:
Price v. Kostryba
(1982),
1982 CanLII 36 (BC SC)
, 70
B.C.L.R. 397 (S.C.).

[
185
] Since that decision, the Court of Appeal has acknowledged accident
victims may indeed incur ongoing subjective psychological injuries causally
connected to the defendant's unlawful act, and that these injuries are
compensable.  In
Maslen v. Rubenstein
(1993),
1993 CanLII 2465 (BC CA)
, 83
B.C.L.R. (2d) 131 (C.A.), the Court of Appeal set out a two part test for
plaintiffs suffering from these types of injuries:

To meet the onus which lies
on a plaintiff in a case of this sort, and thereby avoid the "ultimate
risk of non-persuasion", the plaintiff must, in my view, establish that
his or her psychological problems have their cause in the defendant's unlawful
act, rather than in any desire on the plaintiff's part for things such as care,
sympathy, relaxation or compensation, and also that the plaintiff could not be
expected to overcome them by his or her own inherent resources, or
"will-power".

[
186
] To satisfy the first part of the test, the
plaintiff must negative the proposition that ongoing psychological problems
exist due to some internal subjective cause, such as the plaintiff's desire for
care, sympathy, relaxation, or compensation.

[
187
] In
Skeleton v. Stewart

(1994),
1994 CanLII 3165 (BC CA)
, 93 B.C.L.R. (2d) 200 (C.A.), the Court of Appeal identified the issue
in these cases as:

. . . whether the symptoms
of which a claimant complains are genuine or whether they are motivated by a
desire for financial gain.  For there to be such a desire it surely must be a
conscious one - one which can be controlled or overcome by the claimant.

Simply
put, the fact that the plaintiff's complaints are not organic or physical does
not mean they are not genuine, or that they are motivated by a desire for
compensation.

[
188
] Guidelines for establishing the basis for an
award for psychological injuries causally related to an accident were
summarized in
Yoshikawa v. Yu
,
supra
.   In
that case, the Court of Appeal noted that causation in law applies to
psychological injuries as well as physical injuries.  Lambert J.A. at p.326
outlined the causation test as follows:

. . . First, it must be
shown that the defendant's unlawful act was a "cause-in-fact" of the
plaintiff's psychological symptoms.  That means that the plaintiff must
establish that "but for" the defendant's unlawful act the plaintiff's
psychological symptoms would not have occurred or would not have occurred in
the way they did.  That is a factual question.  Second, it must be shown that
the defendant's unlawful act was a "proximate cause" that is, a
legally relevant cause-in-fact, as a matter of law, of the plaintiff's
psychological symptoms.  That is a legal question.

So if the psychological
symptoms from which the plaintiff is suffering after the accident are symptoms
from which the plaintiff would have been suffering in any event, even if the
defendant's wrongful act had not occurred, then the plaintiff can not meet the
cause-in-fact test and the defendant is not liable for the loss represented by
those symptoms.

But if the psychological
symptoms from which the plaintiff is suffering after the accident would not
have occurred if the defendant's wrongful act had not occurred, then the
cause-in-fact test is met and consideration must be given to the question of "proximate
cause" in law.

[
189
] In addressing the issue of proximate cause, the Court examined the
situation where the plaintiff's own conscious failure to exercise her or his
willpower to bring about a healing of psychological symptoms.  This situation
falls within the principle of
novus actus interveniens

or new intervening acts, and may break the chain of causation;  in such a
situation, the defendant's wrongful act can no longer be said to be the
proximate cause of the injuries.  However, a plaintiff's pre-existing internal
and subjective desire for care, comfort and attention, if entirely unconscious
and contrary to the plaintiff's efforts toward healing psychological symptoms,
does not preclude compensation.  This is simply a restatement of the thin skull
rule:  in a case of pre-existing vulnerability, the wrongdoer must take the
victim as she or he finds him.  As stated by Rowles J.A. at p.352:

.
. . there is no difference in principle between an eggshell skull and an
eggshell personality . . .

[
190
] In addressing the issue of causation for psychological injuries,
Lambert J.A. at p.330 further states:

It
seems to me that there are two different types of psychological symptoms that
may be covered by the principles that are here being discussed.  There are
those where the psychological symptoms have their origin entirely in the
defendant's wrongful act.  Clearly they are compensable.  And there are those
psychological symptoms where the defendant's wrongful act triggers a
pre-existing psychological condition so that both the defendant's wrongful act
and the pre-existing condition are causes-in-fact of the psychological injury.
In the latter cases the psychological injury will be compensable on the basis
of a pre-existing thin skull, except only in cases where the psychological
problem is so dominant as a pre-existing condition and the injuries sustained
in the accident are so trivial that the accident can no longer be said to be a
sufficient cause in law to support an award of damages on the basis of
proximate cause.

I
have difficulty accepting that there will be any cases in which it could be
said that damages should be refused on the basis that the injury suffered in
the accident was merely the subject on which the victim's mind has happened to
focus or fixate, when it cannot also be said that if the accident had not
happened something else would have provided the trigger for the focusing or
fixating so that the psychological symptoms would have occurred in any event
and the cause-in-fact test would not have been met.

[
191
] Subsequently, in
Athey
v. Leonati
,
1996 CanLII 183 (SCC)
, [1996] 3 S.C.R. 458, the Supreme Court of Canada further
clarified the principle of causation at law.  The appeal involved the
application of the thin skull rule.  Pre-existing latent back problems were
aggravated by the defendant's negligence.  The plaintiff suffered a disc
herniation following the accident.  There was no indication that the herniation
ever would have occurred without the negligence of the defendant.  Even though
the accident was not the sole or immediate cause of the disc herniation, because
it played a causative role, the defendant was held to be fully liable.  As
summarized in the headnote:

Causation is established
where the plaintiff proves to the civil standard that the defendant caused or
contributed to the injury.  The general, but not conclusive, test for causation
is the "but for" test, which requires the plaintiff to show that the
injury would not have occurred but for the negligence of the defendant.  Where
the "but for" test is unworkable, the courts have recognized that
causation is established where the defendant's negligence "materially
contributed" to the occurrence of the injury.  In some circumstances an
inference of causation may be drawn from the evidence without positive
scientific proof.  The plaintiff need not establish that the defendant's
negligence was the sole cause of the injury.  The law does not excuse a
defendant from liability merely because other causal factors for which he or
she is not responsible so helped produce the harm.  It is sufficient if the
defendant's negligence was a cause of the harm.

[
192
] The same principles apply to a pre-existing
psychological condition or "eggshell personality".

[
193
] Mr. Gindis' pre-existing condition, which included certain
psychological personality traits and physical low back pain, was aggravated and
exacerbated by the soft tissue injury from the accident.  The resulting
interplay of the pre-existing and post accident symptoms created in Mr. Gindis
a condition of chronic pain.  This chronic pain syndrome requires professional
intervention if Mr. Gindis is not to be written off as a functioning and
productive member of society.  I am satisfied that CPS would not have occurred
in the normal course of events in the absence of the defendant's negligence.

[
194
] Mr. Gindis' continuing refusal to follow the advice of virtually all
the health care professionals who have seen and/or treated him, to exercise
regularly and increase his physical activity, has undoubtedly contributed to
his present state.  Had he exercised regularly from the date of the accident, I
expect that he would not be experiencing the significant debilitating symptoms
that make up CPS to the same degree .  However, I.C.B.C. must also accept some
responsibility for Mr. Gindis' deconditioning.  In my opinion, it failed in its
duty to arrange for Mr. Gindis to participate in a work hardening program soon
after the accident.

[
195
] Had Mr. Laws delayed the settling of Mr. Gindis' claim until he was
able to attend a work hardening program, Mr. Gindis might well have been
rehabilitated back into the work force.  It seems apparent that without such a
program, Mr. Gindis was doomed to frustration and long term unemployment as was
predicted by Dr. Richards.

[
196
] The medical reports before and immediately after the Release was
signed indicated that Mr. Gindis was beginning to suffer from CPS.  Because of
the Release, that condition remained untreated and Mr. Gindis' condition
worsened.  It has significantly diminished the quality and enjoyment of his
life.  A work hardening program shortly after the accident would have impressed
upon Mr. Gindis the important role physical activity played in avoiding his
present deconditioning.

[
197
] Having considered the principles of mitigation as outlined in
Janiak v. Ippolito
,
1985 CanLII 62 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 146, and their
application in
Watters v. Rose
[Q.L.
1993 B.C.J.
No. 216
] (B.C.S.C.), in the circumstances of this case, I would reduce any
quantum of non-pecuniary damages by ten percent.

[
198
] My assessment of Mr. Gindis' non-pecuniary damages is $75,000, less
ten percent for his failure to mitigate, for a total of $67,500.  This
assessment of his non-pecuniary damages is independent of the other heads of
damage.

[
199
] This assessment shows that the bargain on June 3, 1991 was not fair,
just and reasonable.

[
200
] Accordingly, I set aside the Release.

(c)
QUANTUM

[
201
] I find that Mr. Gindis is entitled to compensation under the following
heads of damages:

(i)    Non-pecuniary Damages

[
202
] I award Mr. Gindis $67,500 for pain and suffering, loss of amenities
of life, and loss of enjoyment of life.

(ii)   Special Damages

[
203
] I understand there remains unpaid to Mr. Gindis special damages of
approximately $88.  He is awarded that sum.

(iii)  Future Care Costs

[
204
] In order for Mr. Gindis to reintegrate back into society, he requires
attendance at the Vancouver Pain Clinic at an estimated cost of $11,850.  He
also requires a minimum of 26 one hour psychotherapeutic counselling sessions
at a cost of $155 per visit.  Rounded off, I award Mr. Gindis future care costs
of $15,000.

(iv)   Past Income Loss

[
205
] Mr. Gindis' past income loss from the date of the accident to the date
of trial is difficult to determine given his limited work record.  In the years
1988, 1989, and 1990, he had combined employment and unemployment income of
$11,939, $15,934 (including WCB claim of $1,993.20), and $12,021 respectively.
As the accident occurred on July 7, 1990, the taxation year 1990 reflected only
six months income.

[
206
] Because of his ongoing low back pain, Mr. Gindis decided prior to the
accident to change his employment from a welder/fabricator to less physically
demanding employment.  His low back pain from the WCB accident caused him to be
unable to properly complete two jobs.  His job at Canadian caused him
sufficient low back pain that he had to return to physiotherapy.

[
207
] Given Mr. Gindis' work history, I am not prepared to estimate his past
income loss based on continued full time employment with Sonic as a
welder/fabricator.  I find that Mr. Gindis could reasonably have expected to
continue to have a combination of employment and unemployment earnings, after
the accident, of approximately $15,000 per annum.  As such, I accept the
November 18, 1996 report by PETA Consultants Ltd. ("PETA").  Mr.
Tauton, an analyst with PETA, estimated past income loss to the date of trial
at $90,802.  This is based on the premise of continued earnings consistent with
Mr. Gindis' known earnings history prior to the accident of approximately
15,000 per annum.  It also assumes Mr. Gindis was not able to work during this
period.

[
208
] However, I also find that though he suffered from CPS,  Mr. Gindis was
able to seek light employment after December 1990.  Mr. Gindis admitted this
several times during his cross examination.  His cognitive difficulties were
not sufficient to prevent him from seeking out benefits from various
organizations.  He was extremely focused on that search.  He travelled to
Russia for six months in 1993, for both business and personal reasons.  He was
also focused enough to successfully complete the 18 week NOW program in 1994
and 14 computer courses with the Vancouver School Board in 1995.

[
209
] In May of 1996, after Erik's birth, Mr. and Mrs. Gindis decided that
Mr. Gindis would remain at home and care for Erik when Mrs. Gindis returned to
work in January 1997.  From the time that decision was made, Mr. Gindis has not
looked for light employment.

[
210
] In my opinion, since January of 1991 when Mr. Gindis stated he was
able to return to some form of light employment, he has not made sufficient
efforts to obtain that employment.

[
211
] As a result of the finding that he had the ability to obtain light
employment but chose not to do so, I reduce Mr. Gindis' projected past income
loss of $90,802 by 50%, resulting in a sum of $45,401.  This latter sum is
subject to Court ordered interest and the deduction of CPP disability benefits
received by Mr. Gindis after the accident.

(v)    Future Income Loss

[
212
] Mr. Tauton prepared a further report that estimates the future income
loss Mr. Gindis will suffer to age 65 at $240,234.00.  This estimate assumes
the following:

1)   Mr. Gindis would have continued in the work pattern he
had established prior to the occurrence of the accident.  This pattern included
occasional welding and fabricating jobs, UIC and other benefits.  The annual
income Mr. Gindis would have earned in this pattern is approximately $15,304.

2)   Mr. Gindis' income would not have increased in future
years.

3)   Mr. Gindis is and will remain completely unemployable
due to the injuries he suffered in the accident.

[
213
] I accept the first two assumptions; I do not accept the third.

[
214
] I am optimistic that Mr. Gindis will enjoy some future residual income
earning ability if he chooses to tap into the residual income earning capacity
that he has admitted he has possessed since January 1991.  I make that
statement also based upon the courses Mr. Gindis has now completed and the work
hardening program he intends to take in the near future.  At this time he is
able to do some light sedentary employment.  He has chosen not to pursue that
employment, choosing instead to remain at home to care for his young son.  I
recognise that this is a legitimate lifestyle choice, but it is not one for
which the defendant is obliged to pay.

[
215
] Although I have no figures before me estimating the income Mr. Gindis
will be able to earn doing the degree of light sedentary work that I am
convinced he is able to do, or soon will be, capable of doing, I find that his
residual income earning ability is approximately 50%.  Therefore, based on all
of the above, I reduce the future loss estimate by 50%, for a total of
$121,117.
